strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer vision problem: extending concept-based interpretation from image classification to spatial tasks. Combining localized sparse representations, discovered concept relationships, and language-based naming provides a useful unified framework for classification, segmentation, and captioning.

Downstream evaluation is broad and supports the claim that the concept bottleneck preserves substantial predictive utility. CFM achieves 78.9% ImageNet and 55.4% Places365 accuracy; its average segmentation mIoU is 41.3 versus 41.4 for CLIP-DINOiser, and captioning metrics are similarly close to the opaque backbone. Acceptance need not depend on improving these benchmark scores.

The spatial interpretability results are encouraging. In Fig. 3, CFM improves PartImageNet localization from PatchSAE's 32.2 to 44.3 and COCO-Stuff localization from 34.6 to 44.5, with corresponding improvements in consistency and impurity. The supplementary comparisons against global concept methods further substantiate the benefit of localized representations.

The substantial human study complements automatic metrics, and the appendix documents participant selection, compensation, controls, and frequency-stratified sampling. Training details, vocabulary sources, qualitative failures, and dictionary-size and sparsity ablations also improve transparency.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the main proposed contributions. Tables B1–B3 vary dictionary size and sparsity, but do not separately test DINOising, the Matryoshka objective, relationship discovery, hierarchy-aware naming, vocabulary expansion, and grammatical templates. In particular, naming comparisons change both the representation and naming pipeline. Matched comparisons using the same vocabulary and backbone, with and without hierarchy-aware reconstruction, are needed to establish what the new components contribute beyond the integration of existing methods.

The hierarchy construction has an unresolved technical problem. Equation (2) sums parent activations in the numerator but child activations in the denominator, so its value need not lie in [0,1] or represent a conditional probability. A large parent activation can produce a strong edge despite infrequent co-occurrence. Appendix B.3 repeats this definition without explaining normalization and asserts that the resulting graph is typically a DAG without reporting cycle handling or graph statistics. This affects a central claimed contribution; it is important to establish whether the equation or the implemented procedure is incorrect.

The human evaluation establishes weaker properties than several claims imply. The relationship task asks whether two concepts are related, rather than testing parent–child direction, specialization, or part–whole correctness. The consistency study examines only the five most activating images and does not compare against competing methods. Human naming evaluation compares CFM with random labels, while the stronger baseline comparisons rely on an automated judge without reported human calibration. These results support semantic coherence, but do not fully validate hierarchy accuracy or faithful concept naming across ordinary activations.

Preserving task accuracy does not establish faithful explanations for every downstream task. Captioning uses reconstructed features followed by a nonlinear adapter and language model; evidence for interpretation is limited to selected interventions without aggregate removal success, collateral-change measurements, or random-intervention controls. Figure C15 even replaces the removed pizza with a sandwich/hot dog and changes other scene details. The claim of explanations for all downstream vision tasks therefore exceeds the demonstrated evidence.

Several specification inconsistencies hinder reproducibility. Equations (3)–(4) minimize cosine similarity, whereas Appendix B correctly maximizes it; the weighted reconstruction in Eq. (B.8) also differs materially from the main-text formula. The per-concept 'k-th largest activation' inference threshold in B.5 is insufficiently explained as an approximation to batch-wide TopK sparsity. The cosine-sign error appears readily correctable, but the actual naming and thresholding procedures need an unambiguous specification.

strengths: CFM addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: extending concept-based representations beyond image classification to spatial predictions and captioning. The integration of localized sparse concepts, relationship discovery, and automatic naming is useful, even though its main architectural components build on existing methods.

The grounding results are substantial. In Fig. 3, CFM improves locality over PatchSAE from 32.2 to 44.3 on PartImageNet and from 34.6 to 44.5 on COCO-Stuff, with improvements in consistency and impurity as well. Appendix C also compares against global concept models equipped with post-hoc attribution.

The downstream experiments support a favorable accuracy–interpretability tradeoff. Segmentation averages 41.3 mIoU versus 41.4 for CLIP-DINOiser, classification remains competitive, and the matched captioning experiment reports nearly unchanged quality. Achieving the highest benchmark accuracy is unnecessary for this contribution.

The evaluation combines annotation-based metrics, qualitative examples, automated naming assessment, and a substantial human study with approximately 1,000 questions per task. The appendix provides considerable training and evaluation detail, and the discussion appropriately acknowledges remaining naming limitations.
weaknesses: The hierarchy construction has an unresolved technical problem. Equation (2) calls C_ij a conditional probability in [0,1], but its numerator sums parent activations while its denominator sums child activations. This ratio can exceed one and depends on relative activation magnitudes; exceeding 0.75 does not establish that the parent is usually active whenever the child is active. Thresholding also does not guarantee an acyclic hierarchy. Appendix B.3 repeats the definition without resolving these issues. Because the graph supports both relationship claims and naming, this is consequential rather than merely notational.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed improvements. Appendix B.8 varies dictionary size and sparsity, but does not ablate DINOising, the Matryoshka objective, hierarchy-aware naming, vocabulary expansion, or grammatical templates. In particular, naming comparisons use different concept representations and vocabularies, so they cannot establish how much the proposed hierarchy contributes. Matched comparisons using the same features, vocabulary, and naming procedure would substantially strengthen the scientific case.

The human relationship evaluation measures a weaker property than the claimed hierarchy. Figure A3 explicitly says that concept order does not matter, whereas validating parent–child relationships requires checking direction and distinguishing specialization or part relations from general association. The study supports semantic relatedness, but does not establish the correctness of the extracted hierarchy. Human consistency and naming evaluations also lack matched competing-method conditions.

The evidence for faithful downstream explanations is incomplete. Caption interventions are illustrative examples, without aggregate intervention success or preservation-of-unrelated-content measurements. Appendix B.7 defines segmentation contributions as activation times dictionary–text cosine similarity, but does not establish their exact relationship to the prediction, including decoder-vector norms, decoder bias, and reconstructed-feature normalization. Moreover, Fig. 5's automated naming accuracy remains below 50%, despite clear relative improvements. These results support useful concept interfaces more strongly than the broad claim of transparent explanations for all downstream tasks.

Several specification inconsistencies impede reproducibility. Equations (3)–(4) minimize cosine similarity, whereas Appendix B.4 correctly maximizes it; the appendix's actual naming formula additionally introduces confidence weights, activation weights, and an empirical coefficient absent from the main formulation. Threshold estimation is also unclear, particularly the per-concept 'k-th largest activation' description in B.5. The argmin error alone is readily correctable, but the implemented graph and naming procedure need an unambiguous specification.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: extending concept-based interpretability beyond image classification to spatial prediction and captioning. The combination of localized sparse concepts, discovered relationships, and automatic naming forms a coherent contribution under Algorithms/General.

Downstream evaluation is broad and supports the practical usefulness of the representation. CFM preserves average segmentation performance closely relative to CLIP-DINOiser (41.3 versus 41.4 mIoU), achieves competitive classification accuracy, and approximately matches its backbone on three captioning metrics. Preserving performance while adding interpretable structure is valuable independently of achieving state-of-the-art accuracy.

Concept-quality results are encouraging. Figure 3 reports substantial localization improvements over PatchSAE on PartImageNet and COCO-Stuff, alongside improvements in consistency, impurity, and C2-Score. The human studies provide complementary evidence, with concepts sampled across activation-frequency bins rather than solely selected examples.

The supplement provides extensive training and evaluation details, study instructions, vocabulary sources, dictionary-size and sparsity experiments, and qualitative examples. The explicit discussion and illustration of imperfect concept naming are useful and appropriately candid.
weaknesses: The central hierarchy construction has an unresolved mathematical problem. Equation (2) sums parent activation strengths in the numerator but child activation strengths in the denominator. This ratio need not lie in [0,1] and does not establish the claimed conditional probability: a large parent activation on a small fraction of child-active patches can exceed the threshold. Appendix B.3 repeats this definition without resolving the issue. Thresholding also does not guarantee a DAG, and cycle handling is unspecified. Because these relationships drive the proposed naming procedure, this is more consequential than a notation correction unless the implemented computation is clarified and validated.

The experiments do not isolate the main proposed components. Tables B1–B3 vary dictionary size and sparsity, but do not compare otherwise matched models with and without DINOising, the Matryoshka objective, or hierarchy-aware naming. Naming comparisons additionally change the vocabulary and prompting strategy. Consequently, the results establish that the complete system works, but provide limited evidence that the proposed relationship discovery and naming mechanism produce the reported improvements over simpler alternatives.

The human relationship study measures general relatedness, not whether the predicted parent-to-child direction or specialization/part relationship is correct. Naming is compared with random names in the human study, rather than a matched naming baseline without hierarchy reconstruction. The automated concept-presence evaluation supports improvement over prior systems, but Figure 5 still places absolute accuracy below 50%, which warrants more qualified claims about reliable naming.

Captioning performance preservation and a few interventions do not establish transparent reasoning for arbitrary downstream tasks. The captioner consumes reconstructed features through a nonlinear adapter and language model; readable input concepts alone do not explain its generated decisions. Steering lacks aggregate success, specificity, and collateral-change measurements. Figure C15 illustrates this concern: removing pizza concepts also changes descriptions of the person's action and surrounding objects. The claims of explanations for all downstream tasks exceed the demonstrated evidence.

Several implementation descriptions need reconciliation for reproducibility. Equations (3)–(4) minimize cosine similarity, whereas Appendix B correctly maximizes it; the appendix naming rule additionally introduces activation weights and a coefficient absent from the main equation. Appendix B.5's per-concept 'k-th largest activation' threshold is insufficiently specified to reproduce BatchTopK inference. These are potentially correctable, but compound the uncertainty around the hierarchy and naming implementation.
